t: OpenSSL: What OpenSSL Is: The Internet's Crypto
title: OpenSSL: What OpenSSL Is: The Internet's Crypto
description: OpenSSL is the library that secures the internet: TLS for nearly every server, certificate parsing and validation, and the command-line toolkit (s_client, x509, req) every engineer uses. Version 3.x brought the provider architecture — crypto implementations as pluggable modules — which is how PQC algorithms (via oqs-provider) now enter TLS handshakes. Heartbleed taught the world that this library is critical infrastructure; the project's subsequent hardening is the case study in securing it.

title: OpenSSL: TLS 1.3: The Modern Handshake
description: TLS 1.3 removed the handshake's weak options: forward-secret-only key exchange, encrypted handshake after ServerHello, 0-RTT resumption, and a short list of strong cipher suites. OpenSSL's s_client shows the negotiated version and suite — the check every deployment deserves. The 1.3 handshake is also where PQC enters: hybrid key-exchange groups negotiated like any other, via the provider.

title: OpenSSL: Providers: Pluggable Cryptography
description: OpenSSL 3's providers separate algorithm implementations from the core: the default provider, the FIPS provider (validated module for compliance), and third-party providers like oqs-provider for PQC. Applications request algorithms by name; the provider supplies them. This is how PQC deploys without forking OpenSSL — and how the FIPS boundary stays clean. Provider configuration is now part of every deployment's crypto story.

title: OpenSSL: Certificates: X.509 in Practice
description: OpenSSL's X.509 tooling — req, ca, x509, verify — runs the world's PKI plumbing: CSRs, chains, expiry checks, name constraints. The operational wisdom is automation (ACME/Let's Encrypt for public, internal CA automation for private) and monitoring (expiry alerts, because expired certs still cause outages). With PQC, the practice extends to bigger keys and composite certificates — the tooling handles it, the planning must account for it.

t: OpenSSL: Your First s_client: Reading a Handshake
title: OpenSSL: Your First s_client: Reading a Handshake
description: The hello-world: 'openssl s_client -connect example.com:443' — read the certificate chain, the negotiated TLS version and cipher, the session details. Then '-groups' to offer PQC hybrids with oqs-provider loaded. Every TLS debugging session starts here: the handshake, narrated by the tool. Learning to read s_client output is learning to see what the encryption actually negotiated.

t: OpenSSL: Building OpenSSL: Versions and Configuration
title: OpenSSL: Building OpenSSL: Versions and Configuration
description: OpenSSL is configured at build time: ./Configure with options (no-deprecated, no-weak-ciphers), the FIPS provider built separately for validated deployments. Version discipline matters — 3.x for providers and PQC, supported releases only. The build flags are security decisions: a binary built with weak ciphers enabled carries them forever. Document the configuration; it is part of the posture.

title: OpenSSL: Hardening: Configuration That Resists
description: OpenSSL hardening is configuration: disable old protocols and weak ciphers, set the cipher string deliberately ('TLS 1.3 suites plus ECDHE'), enable HSTS/OCSP stapling at the server, protect private keys (permissions, HSMs where it matters). The testssl.sh-style scan verifies. Hardening is not paranoia; it is the documented, scanned, maintained posture — reviewed when the threat landscape changes.

title: OpenSSL: Defensive Uses: The Encrypted Estate
description: OpenSSL's defensive value is the encrypted estate: every service with modern TLS, every certificate monitored, PQC migrating by plan. The library is also the incident tool — s_client during outages, x509 during cert incidents. An estate whose crypto is current, monitored, and migrating is an estate whose communications resist both today's adversaries and tomorrow's quantum ones.

t: OpenSSL: Private Keys: Custody and Care
title: OpenSSL: Private Keys: Custody and Care
description: Private keys are the crown jewels: filesystem permissions (0600, root-owned), passphrases where operationally feasible, HSMs for CAs and high-value keys, and rotation on schedule or on suspicion. OpenSSL's pkcs12 and key tooling manage the formats; the procedures manage the risk. A key's compromise response — revoke, rotate, investigate — is the incident playbook everyone hopes not to use.

title: OpenSSL: Debugging: Handshake Failures
description: TLS debugging classics: certificate expired or untrusted (the chain — always check the chain), cipher mismatch (the server's list vs the client's), SNI missing (the server serves the wrong cert), and the middlebox that breaks the handshake. s_client with -msg and -state narrates the failure; the alert number names it. Method: reproduce with s_client, read the alert, fix the named cause.

title: OpenSSL: Performance: TLS at Scale
description: TLS performance: session resumption (tickets or PSK) avoids full handshakes, hardware acceleration (AES-NI, QAT) for bulk crypto, and the PQC handshake sizes in the capacity math. Benchmarks on the serving hardware decide the tuning. The good news: modern TLS is fast — the handshake is rarely the bottleneck, and resumption makes it rarer.
